title: The workflow is the product boundary
excerpt: A feature is rarely one screen. It is a promise that crosses people, services, and time. Start system design by mapping the workflow and its states—not by splitting the UI into tickets.
detailTitle: The workflow is the product boundary
prose:
A product request often arrives as a screen: add a booking form, show a payment status, let an operator assign a parcel. The screen is visible, so it is easy to mistake it for the unit of work. But the product promise rarely ends there. A booking starts on one surface, gets authorized by a service, changes inventory, may wait on a payment provider, and must eventually make sense to a passenger and an operator. The workflow is the boundary that matters.

Start with the state changes

Before choosing components or endpoints, write down the business object and the states it can occupy. A payment might be created, pending, confirmed, failed, reversed, or under review. A booking might be held, confirmed, expired, cancelled, or refunded. Then ask who is allowed to move it between states, what evidence permits the transition, and which other records must change with it.

This is more than a modelling exercise. It reveals product decisions hidden inside apparently small requests. Can a guest retry after a timeout? Does a late provider callback revive an expired booking? Can an operator change a confirmed trip? If two surfaces disagree, which one is authoritative? Those are questions for the product owner and engineering together, because the answer changes both customer experience and system behavior.

Give each fact an owner

A useful design assigns one authoritative owner to each important fact. The mobile app can keep a local draft and show progress, but it should not decide that money settled. A dashboard can request a shipment assignment, but the server should validate tenant, trip, and capacity rules. A notification can announce a booking state; it should not create that state.

That separation costs some convenience. A client may need to wait for the server, and an operator may see a pending state where a prototype would show success immediately. In return, retries and concurrent actions have a place to converge. When the network drops after a successful write, the client can fetch the authoritative outcome rather than guessing whether it should repeat the operation.

Design the handoffs, not only the happy path

For each handoff, document the request, the durable state change, the response, and what happens if either side never sees the other. A provider callback can arrive twice. A staff device can be offline. A user can close the app after tapping pay. The appropriate recovery differs by product: a seat may expire, a transfer may need reconciliation, and an offline reading list can simply remain available on the device.

There is a trade-off here too. Mapping every theoretical state can delay learning and bury a small team in ceremony. I focus first on flows that move money, inventory, identity, or a user-visible promise. For a low-risk preference toggle, a simpler path is often enough. The right amount of design is proportional to the cost of getting the transition wrong.

When a feature request arrives, I ask: what promise is changing, which states and people does it cross, and where does the final truth live? Answering those questions makes the work easier to estimate and harder to mis-scope. It also gives founders a clearer choice: which edge cases are necessary for launch, which can wait, and what risk each deferral carries.

title: Choose the smallest system that protects the promise
excerpt: Architecture is a set of operating costs as much as a code structure. Choose the simplest boundary that keeps the product correct today and leaves a credible path for tomorrow.
detailTitle: Choose the smallest system that protects the promise
prose:
When a company raises money or sees early traction, architecture conversations often jump straight to scale. The word can mean thousands of users, a larger team, more integrations, or simply a product that must not lose a payment. Those are different constraints. Adding infrastructure for an unspecified future can make the current product slower to change without making any customer promise safer.

Architecture has a carrying cost

Every service boundary asks the team to own another deployment path, configuration surface, monitoring target, and failure mode. A queue adds delivery semantics and replay questions. A cache adds invalidation and freshness questions. A separate database adds migrations, backup policy, and cross-boundary consistency work. These tools can be right choices; the cost is that they keep asking for attention after the diagram is drawn.

The comparison is not “monolith versus scale.” It is: which constraint is hurting the product, and what is the least complex change that removes it without creating a more expensive one? A single deployable application can still have clear domain modules, narrow interfaces, and isolated ownership. Those seams let the team learn where separation is valuable before paying for distributed operations.

Separate for a reason you can name

I would consider extracting a component when it needs an independent release cadence, a distinct security boundary, materially different resource limits, or ownership by a team that can operate it. I would also separate a workflow when its failure and recovery rules are genuinely different from adjacent work. “We might scale” is not yet evidence; measured contention, deploy risk, incident patterns, or team coordination pain can be.

Keeping components together has trade-offs. A shared process can make one deployment affect more product areas, and a growing codebase can let boundaries erode. The answer is not to ignore that risk. Make module ownership visible, keep dependencies one-way where practical, and use tests around the business rules that must remain stable. If the boundary keeps being crossed, that is evidence to revisit it.

Buy optionality with explicit seams

A sensible early architecture makes likely change affordable without pretending to know the future. Keep payment-provider details behind an adapter if provider replacement is plausible. Keep tenant context explicit if each company must be isolated. Store durable business events where an audit matters. Avoid introducing a generalized platform for a one-off workflow unless more than one real use case needs it.

The judgment is not “never add complexity.” It is to spend complexity where it buys a named product property: correctness, security, independent delivery, or measured performance. For everything else, choose the option the current team can understand, observe, and repair. A small team needs architecture that protects its attention as much as it protects its data.

Before adopting a new service, I want a short decision record: the constraint, the alternatives, the operating cost, the failure mode, and the signal that would justify changing course. That record gives founders a way to revisit the choice when the business changes. Good architecture does not eliminate future decisions; it makes today’s decision legible and tomorrow’s revision possible.

title: Money and inventory run on different clocks
excerpt: A payment provider and a booking database do not share one transaction. Treating them as if they do creates ambiguous outcomes. Model the states, retries, expiry, and reconciliation explicitly.
detailTitle: Money and inventory run on different clocks
prose:
A customer presses pay for the last seat. The provider charges the card, but the response times out before the application records confirmation. The seat hold expires a moment later. Now money and inventory tell different stories, and neither a loading spinner nor a database transaction can make the outside payment provider part of the same atomic commit.

Model the uncertainty explicitly

Start by separating the states: an order can be awaiting payment, confirmed, expired, cancelled, or awaiting reconciliation; a provider payment can be initiated, authorized, captured, failed, or reversed. The exact vocabulary depends on the provider and business rules. The important point is that “request timed out” is not equivalent to “payment failed.” It means the caller does not know yet.

Give each customer intent a stable identifier and make repeated requests resolve to the same intent. Verify provider callbacks on the server, check amount and currency against the order, and make callback processing safe to repeat. A database uniqueness constraint or conditional update should enforce the critical invariant; an application-level “check then insert” can race when two requests arrive together.

Decide what happens at expiry

A seat hold needs an expiry because inventory cannot be reserved forever while a payment is uncertain. But the expiration duration is a product decision: too short and slow or interrupted customers lose a fair chance; too long and inventory is unavailable to everyone else. Choose a defensible starting value using payment latency and customer behavior, then measure how often holds expire and whether those sessions later complete.

At confirmation, the server must check that the hold is still valid and the resource remains available. If payment succeeded after the resource was released, do not silently attach the payment to a different booking. Keep the mismatch visible as a durable state that can trigger a refund, an alternative, or a support review—according to a rule the business has chosen. It is safer to expose an unresolved state than to report success that the records cannot support.

Build for repair as well as prevention

Retries and idempotency prevent many duplicate effects, but they do not guarantee that every provider event arrives or that every timeout resolves quickly. A reconciliation process should compare internal pending records with provider status, record what it checked, and route ambiguous cases to a human rather than rewriting history. Support teams need a shared view of order, payment, provider reference, and last transition.

This design costs more than a one-call checkout. It introduces intermediate states, a callback handler, retry rules, and operational views. For a low-risk action with no money or scarce inventory, that may be disproportionate. For a paid booking, the cost of ambiguity is often a duplicate charge, a stranded customer, or a manual accounting investigation, so the extra state is part of the product.

The useful founder question is not “Can we make checkout instant?” It is “What will the customer see if the charge succeeds and our confirmation does not?” Once that answer is clear, the engineering design can protect it—and the team can measure how often the uncertain path actually occurs.

title: Offline is a product contract, not a cache
excerpt: A cached screen does not make a product work without a network. Decide what remains usable, what must wait for the server, and how a person can tell which state is current.
detailTitle: Offline is a product contract, not a cache
prose:
“The app should work offline” sounds like one requirement. It is several different promises hiding in one sentence. A person may need to read content on a train, check a ticket at a dock, record a field action in a dead zone, or submit a payment while the connection flickers. Those situations do not have the same correctness rules. Caching a screen only addresses the first few seconds of the experience; it does not define what the product is allowed to do.

Separate offline reads from offline writes

Offline reading is often a bounded problem: download a known set of content, store it locally, show when it was last refreshed, and define how storage is replaced. Offline writes are harder. If a staff member records a boarding action without connectivity, the device and server temporarily disagree. Another staff member may record a conflicting action before either device reconnects.

For each offline action, decide whether it is permitted, how it is queued, how it is identified for safe replay, and what happens if the server rejects it later. The interface should distinguish “saved on this device” from “accepted by the business system.” That distinction is not a technical footnote; it changes what a worker can promise to a passenger standing in front of them.

Choose a conflict rule the business can explain

Some data can use last-write-wins without serious harm, such as a locally changed display preference. Inventory, payment, identity, and operational check-ins generally cannot. They may need server validation, explicit conflict resolution, or a rule that prevents a risky action while offline. The user may find that limitation frustrating, but a clear “cannot confirm this yet” is more trustworthy than showing a green success state that another surface will later contradict.

Offline scope also has a cost. Local persistence creates migration, encryption, deletion, and synchronization work. Background sync is constrained by operating systems and battery policies. Keeping every record forever is not a harmless fallback. For a small team, it can be better to make one high-value journey available offline and keep the rest honest about the connection.

Design for recovery when the device returns

A robust sync path records the operation, its stable identity, its local timestamp, and the result of server acceptance. It can retry transient network failures without duplicating effects, surface permanent validation errors, and give the user a way to resolve conflicts that require judgment. The server remains authoritative for shared state; the device remains responsible for preserving the person’s work until it can be reconciled.

Then test the uncomfortable transitions: app killed after the local save, device storage nearly full, account signed out before sync, server rule changed while the device was offline, and two devices making incompatible edits. You do not need to support every case at launch. You do need to choose which ones you support and what the product says about the rest.

The product question is precise: what must this person still be able to do without a signal, and what must the system refuse to pretend it has confirmed? Answering that question produces a smaller, safer offline feature—and gives the team a testable contract instead of a vague cache request.

title: Instrument the decision, not the dashboard
excerpt: Observability earns its cost when it helps the team choose a next action. Connect technical signals to a business workflow, define thresholds, and make the unknown states visible.
detailTitle: Instrument the decision, not the dashboard
prose:
Teams often add analytics after launch by collecting whatever events are easy to emit. The dashboard grows, but the founder still cannot answer the question they actually have: are customers completing the workflow, and where do they get stuck? Telemetry is useful when it changes a decision. Without that link, it is a second product to maintain and a pile of numbers that look precise without being actionable.

Start with a decision you may need to make

Write down a business question and the action that a possible answer would trigger. If checkout abandonment rises, would the team shorten the form, change payment instructions, or investigate provider latency? If expired booking holds increase, would you adjust the timeout, inspect a payment step, or improve the warning shown to the customer? If every possible result leads to “keep watching,” the measurement may not yet justify its cost.

Then define an event around the business transition, not around the button tap. “Payment started” and “booking confirmed” should have clear meanings, stable identifiers, and timestamps. Record enough context to join the journey across mobile request, API, background worker, and provider callback, while excluding payment credentials and unnecessary personal data. Correlation is what lets an engineer tell a slow provider from a lost callback or a user who abandoned checkout.

Pair product outcomes with system signals

A completion rate alone may hide the cause of a change. Pair it with a small set of diagnostic signals: request latency, provider timeouts, duplicate callback count, queue age, and unresolved payment states. For search, pair result engagement with latency and zero-result rates. For notifications, distinguish accepted by provider from opened or acted upon. Each signal has a different meaning; one green delivery response does not prove a person saw the message.

Set a threshold that has an owner and a next action. For example, a growing count of payments awaiting reconciliation can page an operator before it becomes a customer complaint. A rise in offline sync conflicts may be a product design issue, not a server scaling issue. Thresholds will be imperfect at first. Their job is to make attention deliberate, then improve from observed patterns.

Measure honestly and protect the team’s attention

Do not call a provider request “delivered” unless the provider defines it that way. Do not infer revenue impact from clicks without a defensible link to completed transactions. Keep instrumentation proportional: high-risk transitions deserve stronger audit trails and alerts than an optional profile decoration.

There is a trade-off between detailed observability and overhead. More events can help diagnose a rare failure, but they also create cost, privacy exposure, retention obligations, and maintenance work. A small team should start with the few journeys whose failure has a meaningful business consequence, then expand as evidence shows a blind spot.

The standard I use is simple: can a teammate tell what happened, who or what was affected, and what action comes next? If the answer requires joining unrelated dashboards by hand, the observability design has not finished its product work. Make the signal serve an operating decision, and the dashboard becomes a tool rather than a deliverable.
